sections.text:
A church writes to Paul, and Paul has also heard from Chloe's household that there are contentions among them. One says, “I follow Paul”, another “I follow Apollos”. That is the church in Corinth: gifted, lively and troubled. 1 Corinthians is Paul's answer to the reports and the questions.

He deals with rival groups, a case of sexual immorality, lawsuits between believers, marriage and singleness, food offered to idols, behavior in worship and abuses at the Lord's Supper. None of it is abstract. Each problem is a real quarrel among people who gather for worship.

In chapters 12 to 14 he discusses spiritual gifts, and the chapter on love sits at the center, ending with the words, “The greatest of these is love.” Then in chapter 15 he rests everything on one claim: that Christ died, was buried and was raised on the third day. It is the Bible's longest treatment of the resurrection, of Christ and of those who belong to him.

Corinth was a wealthy port city in Greece, and Paul had started the church there. He wrote this letter from Ephesus around the year 54 or 55, in answer to reports that had reached him and questions the church had put to him.

Christians differ on whether gifts such as tongues and prophecy continue today. The passages on women in worship (chapters 11 and 14) are read differently: some see lasting instructions, others guidance for a particular situation. Most readers agree that the instruction about head coverings reflects the customs of the time, while differing on the principle behind it.

News has reached Paul from the household of Chloe, and it is not good. The church in Corinth is splitting into camps. One says he follows Paul, another Apollos, a third Cephas, a fourth Christ. Paul answers with three sharp questions. “Is Christ divided?” Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized into Paul’s name?

The cure he offers is the cross. To those who are perishing it sounds like foolishness, but to those being saved it is the power of God. Jews ask for signs and Greeks look for wisdom, but Paul preaches Christ crucified.

He then asks them to look at themselves. Not many of them were wise or mighty or of noble birth. God chose the weak and lowly so that no one could boast. “He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”

Paul wrote this letter to a church he had helped found in Corinth, a busy port city. It is usually dated about the middle of the 50s, written while he was in Ephesus. The letter answers reports and a list of questions from the church itself, and its first concern is unity. Paul names himself among those who should not be made into party leaders. The chapter sets the keynote for the letter: the cross overturns human ideas of wisdom and status. See 1 Corinthians 2 and 3.

Paul remembers how he first came to Corinth, and he does not dress it up. He did not arrive with fine speech or clever wisdom. “I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.” He was there “in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling.” His message came with the power of the Spirit, so that their faith would rest on God’s power and not on human wisdom.

Still, he says, there is a wisdom he speaks among the mature. It is God’s wisdom, hidden and prepared before the ages. The rulers of this age did not know it, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

He explains how it reaches people. No one knows a person’s thoughts except that person’s spirit, and no one knows God’s thoughts except God’s Spirit. God has given his Spirit so that believers can understand what God has freely given. The chapter ends: “we have Christ’s mind.”

This chapter continues Paul’s answer to the divisions described in 1 Corinthians 1. Some in Corinth prized impressive speakers and clever ideas, so Paul recalls what his own visit actually looked like. The phrase “the natural man” in verse 14 is read in different ways. Some take it to mean any person without the Spirit, others a believer who is acting in a worldly way. Christians also differ on whether the “rulers of this world” are human authorities, spiritual powers, or both.

Paul has to say something that no teacher likes to say. He could not speak to the Corinthians as to spiritual people, but as to babies in Christ. He fed them milk because they were not ready for solid food, and jealousy and quarreling show that they are still not ready.

He asks who Apollos is and who Paul is. They are servants through whom the Corinthians believed. “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.”

Then the picture changes from a field to a building. Paul laid a foundation, and no one can lay another besides Jesus Christ. Others build on it with gold and silver or with wood, hay and straw, and the Day will show what each has built. Fire will test it.

Then comes a line to the whole church: “you are God’s temple”. The word “you” is plural, and the closing words are the heart of the chapter: all things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.

Paul writes to a church in which people lined up behind favorite teachers (see 1 Corinthians 1). The fire in verses 12 to 15 is read in different ways. Many Protestants see a judgment of believers’ work, and many Catholics have seen in it support for purgatory. Others stress that it is the work, not the person, that is tested. The temple language here is aimed first at the church as a community, though later chapters speak of the individual body as well. See 1 Corinthians 6.

Paul asks the Corinthians to see him and Apollos plainly: as Christ’s servants and stewards of God’s mysteries. “it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” He tells them that being judged by them, or by any human court, is a very small thing to him. He does not even judge himself, and the one who judges him is the Lord. So they should judge nothing before the time.

Then he turns with some irony on their pride. “And what do you have that you didn’t receive?” They act as though they already reign, while the apostles are on display like men sentenced to death, hungry, beaten and homeless. Paul says he blesses when cursed and endures when persecuted.

But he says that he writes as a father, not to shame them. He is sending Timothy. And he ends with a choice for them to make: “Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?”

This chapter closes Paul’s long opening argument about divisions in the church. Corinth was a city that valued status, and some of the believers evidently liked the sense of being spiritually advanced. Paul does not defend himself but points to the pattern of Christ’s own humility. Timothy, mentioned here, is described in the book of Acts as Paul’s younger coworker. The father image in verses 14 to 17 is meant tenderly, as the stress on love shows. See 2 Corinthians 2 for how the relationship develops.

Paul has heard something shocking and he does not soften it. There is sexual immorality in the church of a kind not even found among the Gentiles: a man is with his father’s wife. What troubles Paul as much as the act is that the church is proud instead of mourning.

He tells them to gather and remove the man from among them. He uses a household picture. “a little yeast leavens the whole lump”. Old yeast must be cleared out before Passover, and Paul says that “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed in our place.” So the church should keep the feast with sincerity and truth.

He then clears up a misunderstanding about an earlier letter. He never meant that they should avoid the immoral people of the world, for then they would have to leave the world. He meant those who call themselves brothers and live this way. The outsiders God will judge. The insiders the church must deal with.

The phrase “deliver such a one to Satan” is hard. Most readers understand it as putting the man out of the church, back into the world where Satan rules, with the hope that he will come to his senses. Many link it to the later teaching in 2 Corinthians 2 about forgiving and restoring someone who has repented, though scholars debate whether the same man is meant. The chapter is about discipline inside a community that has chosen to follow Christ. It does not authorize judgment of outsiders.

Paul is amazed at what he hears. Believers are taking one another to court before unbelievers. Surely, he says, the saints will judge the world, so can they not settle small matters among themselves? Better to be wronged than to wrong a brother.

Then he gives a list of those who will not inherit the Kingdom of God, among them the greedy, thieves, drunkards, idolaters and the sexually immoral. And he adds a sentence of hope: “Some of you were such, but you were washed.” They were also sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus.

He next takes up a slogan, “All things are lawful for me,” and says not everything helps. The body, he says, is for the Lord and not for sexual immorality. Bodies are members of Christ, and the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. “you were bought with a price.” So honor God with your body.

The list in verses 9 and 10 includes two words, rendered in this translation as male prostitutes and homosexuals, whose exact meaning scholars and Christians debate. Some hold that they refer to same-sex behavior in general, and others that they refer to particular practices such as exploitation. Verse 11 matters for how the list is read, since Paul says the church was made up of people who had been washed. Corinth was known for its commerce and temples, which formed the setting for his warnings about sexual immorality.

The Corinthians had written Paul a letter, and here he begins answering it. They had asked about marriage, and some seem to have said it is good for a man not to touch a woman. Paul grants that but says that, because of temptation, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Each owes the other affection. “Likewise also the husband doesn’t have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”

He then speaks to the unmarried, the widowed, married couples and those with an unbelieving spouse. He keeps marking what is the Lord’s command and what is his own judgment. He says it’s “better to marry than to burn with passion”, but also that each has a gift from God.

He tells people to stay in the condition in which they were called. For slaves he adds: “if you get an opportunity to become free, use it.” He closes by advising that the time is short.

This chapter is among the most careful in the New Testament about what Paul says as a command from the Lord and what as his own opinion. He writes in a time he calls one of “distress” and his advice about staying single is tied to that moment. Christians read his words on marriage, divorce, remarriage and singleness differently, and churches have often drawn different lines. Slavery was a fact of Corinthian life. The text shows Paul preferring freedom for those who can get it. See Philemon for the same theme.

Someone in Corinth has asked about meat that was offered to idols. In a city full of temples, it showed up in markets and at feasts, and believers were unsure whether eating it was safe.

Paul starts with what everyone knows: an idol is nothing, and there is only one God. “to us there is one God, the Father,” and one Lord, Jesus Christ. But he adds a warning about how knowledge can be used. “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”

Not everyone has the confidence that an idol is nothing. Some have been used to idols until now, and when they eat, their weak conscience is hurt. So Paul asks the knowing ones to look at it from the other side. If a believer with knowledge sits at a meal in an idol’s temple, a weaker believer may be led to do what he thinks is wrong. His conclusion is personal: “if food causes my brother to stumble, I will eat no meat forever more”.

Meat from temple sacrifices was sold in markets and served at civic and social meals in Corinth, which made this a daily problem. Paul treats it in three chapters: here, in the middle of chapter 9 and again in chapter 10. His approach is to start from the truth about one God and then to weigh it against love for others. Churches have used this chapter to think about freedom and responsibility, about when to give up a right for another person’s sake. See Romans 14 for a related discussion.

Paul begins with questions that sound like a defense. “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?” The Corinthians themselves, he says, are the seal of his apostleship. Then he argues for rights he has chosen not to use. Other apostles and the Lord’s brothers take a believing wife along and live from their work. Soldiers, vine growers and shepherds all share in what they work for, and the law says not to muzzle an ox while it treads the grain. Those who serve at the temple eat from it. In the same way, the Lord ordained that those who preach the Good News should live from it.

But Paul has used none of this. He preaches without charge. For the sake of the gospel he has made himself everyone’s servant: to the Jews like a Jew, to the weak like the weak. “I have become all things to all men”. The chapter ends with a runner who runs “not aimlessly”.

Paul’s example here continues the discussion of giving up rights from 1 Corinthians 8. Some in Corinth seem to have questioned his authority, perhaps because he did not accept payment. The phrase about becoming all things to all men has sometimes been taken as a claim that Paul would say anything to win a hearing. In context it means that he adapted his habits out of love and kept his own faithfulness to Christ. The race and prize picture draws on athletic games, which Corinth hosted.

Paul tells a story the Corinthians already know. Their ancestors in the faith all passed under the cloud and through the sea. They all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink. Yet God was not pleased with most of them, and they fell in the wilderness. Paul recalls their idolatry, their sexual immorality, their testing and their grumbling. These things were examples, and so he warns that anyone who thinks he stands should be careful that he does not fall.

Then comes a promise for the tempted: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able”. There is always a way of escape.

He warns them to flee idolatry. The cup and the bread are a sharing in Christ’s body and blood, and they cannot share that table and the table of demons. On everyday questions he is relaxed. Eat what is sold in the market, for “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” and give no offense to others. “Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.”

This chapter is the third in Paul’s answer about meat offered to idols (1 Corinthians 8 and 9). His readers lived among temples, and a shared meal could carry religious meaning. His references to Israel in the wilderness are found in Exodus and Numbers. Christians understand the Lord’s Supper in different ways, from a memorial to a real presence of Christ, and verses 16 and 17 are part of that conversation. The reference to demons reflects the ancient view that idol worship involved spiritual powers.

Paul opens with praise and a model: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” He praises them for remembering the traditions. Then he takes up two matters in their worship.

The first is about head coverings for men and women who pray or prophesy. Paul’s argument is dense and not easy to follow. He speaks of head, glory, and the order of creation, and then adds a balance: “neither is the woman independent of the man, nor the man independent of the woman, in the Lord.” Both come from God.

The second matter is harsher. When they gather for the Lord’s Supper, the rich eat first and the poor go hungry. Paul recalls what he received: on the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.” So Paul warns them against eating in an unworthy way. His practical word is simple: “Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.”

The first half of this chapter has been read in very different ways, especially on the place of women. Some take Paul’s language about head and order as a lasting pattern. Others see local custom, since a head covering carried particular meanings in Corinth, and read the word “head” as source rather than ruler. The text itself shows women praying and prophesying aloud in worship. The second half holds the earliest written account of the Lord’s Supper in the New Testament. Churches differ on what happens in it.

Paul wants his readers to understand spiritual gifts, and he begins with the thing all believers have in common. No one speaking by God’s Spirit curses Jesus, and no one can say that Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit.

Then he lists the variety. “various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit” various kinds of service, and the same Lord. Wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, languages and their interpretation are given to each person for the good of all.

The picture he uses is the human body. It is one body with many members, and in one Spirit all were baptized into it, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free. The foot cannot say it does not belong because it is not a hand. The eye cannot tell the hand it has no need of it. The weaker members are necessary. “When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.” Paul ends: “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.” Yet he points to a still better way.

The Corinthians had put a high value on certain gifts, especially speaking in other languages, and may have ranked people by them. Paul answers by stressing that all gifts come from one Spirit and are given for the common good. Christians have long differed on whether gifts such as healing and tongues continue today in the same form. The order of the list in verse 28 is also read in different ways. Chapter 13 follows without a break, and the most excellent way Paul promises is the subject of that chapter.

In the middle of a long argument about spiritual gifts, Paul stops and sets down a hymn to love. If he could speak in the languages of men and of angels but had no love, he would be only a clanging cymbal. He could have prophecy, all knowledge, a faith that moves mountains, and give away everything, even his body, but without love he would be nothing.

Then he describes love by what it does. “Love is patient and is kind.” It does not envy or boast, is not proud, does not seek its own way, takes no account of evil, and rejoices with the truth. It bears, believes, hopes and endures all things.

Gifts will pass away. “Love never fails.” For now we know in part, and we see in a mirror, dimly. Then we will see face to face and know fully. The chapter ends on three things that remain: faith, hope and love. “The greatest of these is love.”

This chapter sits between two chapters about spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12 and 14) and is meant to correct how the Corinthians used them. It is often read at weddings, but Paul wrote it for a quarrelsome church, and every line is aimed at their behavior. The words “when that which is complete has come” are read in different ways: as the return of Christ, as the final state of things, or, in some traditions, as the completion of Scripture. The mirror in verse 12 is thought to refer to the polished metal mirrors of the time, which showed a dim reflection.

Paul wants the Corinthians to pursue love and to desire spiritual gifts, and above all to prophesy. His reason is simple. Someone who speaks in another language speaks to God, and no one else understands. Someone who prophesies builds up, encourages and comforts the whole assembly.

He uses pictures from sound. A pipe or harp or trumpet must give a clear note or no one knows what is meant. Speech in the assembly must be clear, or it is speaking into the air. He himself speaks in other languages more than they all, yet in the assembly he would rather speak “five words with my understanding” than ten thousand in another language.

He gives them rules: two or three at the most, in turn, with interpretation. Prophets are to speak one at a time, and the others weigh what is said. He tells wives to be quiet in the assemblies, and he closes by saying “God is not a God of confusion but of peace”. His last line is “Let all things be done decently and in order.”

Verses 34 and 35 are among the most discussed in the letter, since in chapter 11 women pray and prophesy aloud. Some scholars think the verses limit a particular kind of disruption, such as interrupting with questions during the weighing of prophecy. Some think Paul is quoting a Corinthian view. Some think the verses were added later, since a few ancient copies place them elsewhere. Others read them as a lasting rule. Christians also differ on whether tongues continue today.

Paul reminds the Corinthians of the Good News he preached. “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,” was buried, and was raised on the third day. Then he names who saw him: Cephas, the twelve, over five hundred at once, most of them still alive, then James, all the apostles, and last of all himself, “the child born at the wrong time”. He calls himself the least of the apostles because he persecuted the church, yet by grace he is what he is.

Some in Corinth say there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul answers that if that is true, Christ was not raised and their faith is empty. But Christ has been raised, the first fruits. As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. “The last enemy that will be abolished is death.”

He describes the body like a seed that is sown and raised, then tells of a mystery, a trumpet and a change. The chapter ends with a taunt at death, a thanksgiving, and a call to stand firm.

This chapter holds one of the earliest written summaries of the Easter message, in verses 3 to 5, which many scholars think Paul received from earlier believers and passed on. Verse 29, about being baptized for the dead, is obscure, and Christians have proposed many explanations without agreement. The picture of the spiritual body has been read as a real physical body transformed, and also in other ways. Paul’s point throughout is that the resurrection of Christ is the ground of Christian hope.

After the great argument of chapter 15, the letter comes down to earth, and the details are warm. Paul first speaks about a collection for the saints in Jerusalem. On the first day of every week each should set aside something as they prosper, so that nothing needs to be gathered in a rush when he arrives. Those the church approves will carry the gift.

He shares his plans. He will pass through Macedonia, perhaps winter with them, and for now stay at Ephesus until Pentecost, “for a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.” He asks them to welcome Timothy without fear, and reports that Apollos is not yet ready to come.

Then a short charge: “Watch! Stand firm in the faith! Be courageous! Be strong!” And: “Let all that you do be done in love.” He commends the household of Stephanas and sends greetings. He signs with his own hand and ends with the cry “Come, Lord!”

The collection for Jerusalem was important to Paul, and he writes about it in several letters (see Romans 15 and 2 Corinthians 8 and 9). This chapter gives a small window into daily life in early churches, with their travelers, hosts and house gatherings. Some Christians have taken the first day of the week in verse 2 as a sign that believers met for worship on that day. The Aramaic phrase behind “Come, Lord” appears here in Greek letters in many ancient copies and is an early prayer for Christ’s return.
